questions.q: What is the primary dramatic conflict that structures the discussion points in "जतुः", and which two characters embody the opposing poles of this conflict most sharply?
questions.a: The primary conflict is the tension between institutional self-preservation (embodied by the Principal who prioritizes rules, fees, and reputation) and moral accountability (embodied by Jtuh who risks her career to expose systemic cruelty). A wrong answer identifying "student vs. teacher" or "rich vs. poor" reveals the student has reduced the play's systemic critique to interpersonal drama, missing how the Principal's "नियम" and Jtuh's "नियम तोड़ना" represent competing logics of education itself.

questions.q: Explain why Yathyak's mother's shift from defending the coaching system (page 70: "अच्छा ही तो था... कोचिंग में पढ़ते थे") to condemning it (page 83: "फीस के नाम पर... बच्चों की जान ले रहे हैं") is dramatically necessary for the play's argument about complicity.
questions.a: Her transformation demonstrates that complicity is not static villainy but active participation sustained by hope and fear; the play argues that parents become enforcers of the very system that destroys their children because they internalize its metrics (marks, ranks, fees paid) as love. A wrong answer treating her as "hypocritical" or "inconsistent" reveals the student reads character psychologically rather than structurally, missing how the play uses her arc to indict the system's ability to colonize parental love.

questions.q: Using the Grihsevak's testimony (pages 82-83: "दोनों घंटों... बच्चों की जान ले रहे हैं"), construct a discussion prompt that forces participants to confront the play's implication that non-teaching staff often witness institutional violence more clearly than educators.
questions.a: Effective prompt: "The Grihsevak sees 'दोनों तरफ से बच्चों की जान ली जा रही है' while the Principal sees 'नियम'. What does this gap in perception reveal about who is permitted to know what in educational institutions? Cite one moment where a teacher's professional role blinds them to what a servant sees." A weak prompt asking "Is the Grihsevak reliable?" reveals the student treats testimony as factual evidence rather than dramatic perspective, missing the play's epistemic hierarchy critique.

questions.q: Analyze how the play's final stage direction — "सारा मैदान... एक नया आंदोलन का उद्गम" — transforms Jtuh's individual act of whistleblowing into a collective possibility, and why this matters for discussion design.
questions.a: The direction refuses tragic closure (Jtuh's suspension) by staging the aftermath as collective awakening: parents, students, and the Grihsevak converge, suggesting resistance requires crossing the very boundaries (teacher/parent, insider/outsider) the system enforces. Discussion design must therefore move beyond "Was Jtuh right?" to "What alliances does the play imagine as necessary for change?" A response focusing on Jtuh's heroism reveals the student defaults to individual moralism, missing the play's structural insistence that accountability is collective.

questions.q: Evaluate the pedagogical risk of framing the play's coaching critique as "coaching is bad" versus "the coaching industry exploits parental anxiety and institutional vacancy". Which framing better serves the play's complexity and why?
questions.a: The second framing is superior because it preserves the play's systemic analysis: coaching fills a vacuum created by school failure (Principal admits "स्कूल का काम ही है कि शिक्षा के प्रचार-प्रसार में जितना भी हो सके योगदान दे"), and parents choose it desperate for mobility ("गरीब माँ-बाप... फीस देते हैं"). The first framing lets institutions off the hook by making coaching an external villain. A student defending the first framing reveals they read the play as social commentary rather than institutional critique, missing how the Principal's "फीस के नाम पर" indictment implicates the entire educational economy.

questions.q: Create a discussion opening that uses Vafar's silence (pages 72-73: "हूँ... हूँ... देखते क्या हो") as a metaphor for student voicelessness, and requires participants to trace how the play both represents and resists that silence through its dramatic form.
questions.a: Strong opening: "Vafar speaks mostly in grunts and fragmented sentences until Jtuh forces his file open — his silence is the play's central sound. How does the script's structure — overlapping dialogues, stage directions describing bodily collapse, the Grihsevak's testimony — make audible what Vafar cannot say? Identify one moment where the form itself 'speaks' for him." A weak opening asking "Why is Vafar quiet?" reveals the student treats silence as character trait rather than dramatic strategy, missing how the play's polyphonic form (multiple voices, interrupted speeches, offstage sounds) enacts the struggle for voice.
